analysis.one_liner: Ends government reporting of large bank transactions and company owners, requiring search warrants instead.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 16, 2025 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has seen no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip most reporting duties from the Bank Secrecy Act, the anti-money-laundering law now on the books. Banks would no longer automatically report large cash transactions, like transfers over $10,000, to the government, and companies would no longer have to disclose who actually owns them. Instead, federal agencies could get a customer's bank records only with a search warrant.
analysis.who_benefits: People and entities that move large sums of money or own companies through anonymous structures. Eliminating the reports would end the paper trail that investigators currently use to spot money laundering, tax evasion, and the financing of terrorism. Banks also benefit from lower compliance costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large-money movers and anonymous company owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes requirements that financial institutions report certain financial transactions, such as transfers over $10,000, to government agencies, so customers would no longer be flagged automatically for moving large sums.

It restricts government access to customer financial records: agencies could obtain them only through a search warrant, rather than under the broader administrative and subpoena mechanisms now allowed by the Right to Financial Privacy Act.
It eliminates the requirement that companies report their beneficial owners, so the government would no longer automatically learn who actually owns a corporate entity.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement and the public. Investigators would lose the routine transaction reports and beneficial-ownership records they currently use to trace money laundering, tax evasion, and terrorist financing, and would have to know which specific records to seek before getting a warrant.
analysis.who_pays_short: Financial crime investigators and the public

drawbacks.text: The reports being eliminated exist to help detect illicit activity such as money laundering and the financing of terrorism, so ending them removes a core detection tool for financial crime.
Ending beneficial-ownership reporting would make it harder to identify who is behind a company, weakening accountability for entities used to hide money.

Privacy gains under the bill are broad, but the largest privacy changes apply to large cash transactions and company ownership, where the current reporting is aimed at detecting crime rather than monitoring ordinary accounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's warrant requirement is a genuine privacy safeguard for ordinary customers' bank records. But its largest changes go the other way: it ends automatic reporting precisely where the money is large or the ownership is hidden, shifting detection of financial crime onto investigators who would have to know what to look for in advance. On balance the costs to enforcement outweigh the privacy gains for the average person.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which has not held a hearing or brought it to a vote, so nothing has happened to it yet.

narrative.text: Rep. John W. Rose (R-TN) introduced the Bank Privacy Reform Act in the House on January 16, 2025.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
One colleague, Rep. Ogles, cosponsored the bill, and no further legislative action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one: the bill has gone nowhere, leaving current bank reporting rules and warrant limits unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill sits untouched

for.name: Rep. John W. Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bank Privacy Reform Act in the House on January 16, 2025.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 16, 2025 and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans, Rose and Ogles, are attached to the bill, and no votes or opposition statements are on record.

industries.note: The bill ends banks' duties to file reports of large transactions and to supply records to government agencies outside a warrant process, cutting compliance costs and legal exposure. That relief comes with the trade-off that the flows those reports were designed to flag — laundering and terror financing — would be harder to detect in the system banks operate.

By eliminating beneficial-ownership reporting, the bill lets company owners keep their identities off government books. Ordinary people gain nothing from that anonymity; its value is precisely in avoiding detection, including for tax evasion and laundering.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with one cosponsor and no committee action more than a year into the session is on the usual path for a bill like this: it will most likely sit in the Financial Services Committee and expire at the end of the Congress without a vote.
